title: Economic Inequality
scope: Causes and cures of the rich-poor gap. Not wages specifically or wealth taxation.

overview.summary: How far rich-world income and wealth gaps widened, what drove it, and whether the gap itself is the target.
overview.scope_covered: Income and wealth gaps in rich democracies: what widened them, whether the gap itself matters, and which levers would close it.
overview.scope_excluded: Poverty and growth in low-income countries, race and gender pay gaps, and the administration of individual benefit programs.
overview.why_now: A cost-of-living backlash has put affordability at the center of the 2026 election cycle, reopening the argument over what widened the gap and whether closing it is the right goal.

stats.label: Top 1% income share · before tax and transfers
stats.note: The top 1%’s share of pre-tax US national income has roughly doubled since 1980, from about 10% to 20.7% in 2024.
stats.detail: The World Inequality Database builds this series from tax records, surveys and national accounts, the standard method for long-run pre-tax income shares; it measures income before any redistribution, so it says nothing about the picture after taxes and transfers (the Congressional Budget Office series on income after transfers and taxes, below, tracks that). Researchers also debate how much of the post-1980s rise reflects genuine income growth at the top versus a reclassification of business income following the 1986 tax reform, which made it more attractive to report profits as individual rather than corporate income. A second and larger dispute runs over the series itself: Gerald Auten and David Splinter, working from the same IRS records, find a considerably smaller rise in the top 1%’s share than this series shows, and Piketty, Saez and Zucman have answered them in technical notes since 2023.

stats.label: Top 1% wealth share · US households
stats.note: The top 1% of US households held 31.6% of net worth in the first quarter of 2026, just off the record 31.8% and up from 22.8% in 1989.
stats.detail: The Fed’s Distributional Financial Accounts is the official quarterly series for US wealth concentration; wealth shares combine housing, business equity, retirement accounts and financial assets, so they move with asset prices and interest rates as well as with underlying saving and inheritance patterns, making single quarters noisier than the multi-decade upward trend they sit on.

stats.label: Chance of out-earning your parents · by birth cohort
stats.note: 92% of Americans born in 1940 grew up to earn more than their parents at the same age; only 50% of those born in 1984 did.
stats.detail: Chetty and coauthors calculate this ‘absolute mobility’ rate by comparing each child’s household income at about age 30 to their parents’ income at the same age, adjusted for inflation. The decline held across the income distribution and in all 50 states. Their counterfactuals put most of the fall on how growth was shared rather than on how fast it ran: giving the 1980 cohort the 1940 cohort’s GDP growth while dividing it as income is divided today lifts absolute mobility to 62%, closing 29% of the gap, whereas dividing today’s GDP as the 1940 cohort’s was divided lifts it to 80%, closing 71%. Under the current distribution, they estimate it would take sustained real GDP growth above 6% a year to restore mid-century odds.

stats.label: Growth gap between productivity and pay · since 1979
stats.note: US net productivity grew 90.2% between 1979 and 2025, while a typical worker’s pay rose 33.0%.
stats.detail: The Economic Policy Institute compiles the comparison from Bureau of Labor Statistics data, setting net output per hour worked (output less depreciation) against inflation-adjusted compensation, including benefits, for production and nonsupervisory workers. The size of the gap is sensitive to which price index deflates each series, a technical choice economists dispute. Anna Stansbury and Lawrence Summers, who find that a percentage point of productivity growth still passes through to 0.7 to 1 points of median compensation growth, nonetheless document a stark divergence since 1973; critics at the American Enterprise Institute argue the residual gap is largely an artifact of the deflator choice and of measuring wages rather than total compensation.

stats.label: College wage premium · full-time workers
stats.note: Full-time, year-round workers 25 and older with a bachelor’s degree or higher had median earnings 1.8 times those of high school graduates in 2024, up from about 1.7 times in 2004.
stats.detail: Census Bureau data on full-time, year-round earnings by education is the standard official series. Economists including Autor, Goldin and Katz attribute most of the long-run rise to skill-biased technological change outpacing growth in the supply of college graduates. A 2025 San Francisco Fed working paper finds the premium, having grown substantially from the 1980s through the early 2000s, has been largely unchanged in the two decades since, and attributes that stagnation mainly to demand: a slowdown in the pace of skill-biased technological change.

stats.label: Income growth after transfers and taxes · lowest fifth, 1979 to 2022
stats.note: Income after transfers and federal taxes grew at every rung from 1979 to 2022: the bottom fifth roughly doubled, the middle three fifths rose 65%, the top fifth 144%.
stats.detail: The Congressional Budget Office builds this series by matching tax returns to survey data, adding means-tested transfers such as Medicaid, SNAP and the EITC and subtracting federal taxes, which is why it runs well above pre-tax measures for households at the bottom. The endpoint matters: CBO’s previous release stopped at 2021, a year lifted by pandemic relief, and showed a markedly larger gain at the bottom than the 2022 data do. Growth is also steeply skewed inside the top fifth, running fastest for households at the very top of the distribution.
stats.source_label: Congressional Budget Office, The Distribution of Household Income, 2022

stats.label: Union membership rate · US wage and salary workers
stats.note: US union membership halved between 1983 and 2025, from 20.1% of workers to 10.0%.
stats.detail: The Bureau of Labor Statistics has run this series consistently since 1983 using the Current Population Survey. Private-sector density fell further, to 5.9% in 2025, while public-sector density stayed at 32.9%, a divergence institutionalists cite as evidence the decline reflects labor-law and bargaining choices rather than an inevitable shift with the economy.
stats.source_label: US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Union Members — 2025

stats.label: How far taxes and transfers narrow the gap · US vs. peer democracies
stats.note: Cash taxes and transfers narrow the US income gap by about 22%; Belgium, Finland and Ireland narrow theirs by more than 40%.
stats.detail: Compiled from OECD and Luxembourg Income Study data comparing market income to disposable income: on the 2023 figures the reduction runs to about 48% in Belgium and 47% in Finland, 41% in Ireland, 36% in Italy, 30% in the United Kingdom and 29% in Canada, against 22% in the United States. The comparison counts cash taxes and transfers only, so in-kind benefits such as Medicare and Medicaid sit outside it on both sides of the ledger.
stats.source_label: Our World in Data, drawing on OECD and LIS data

stats.label: Households burdened by housing costs · spending over 30% of income
stats.note: In 2024, 22.7 million renter and 20.7 million owner households, 43.4 million in all, spent more than 30% of income on housing, a fourth straight record for renters.
stats.detail: Harvard’s Joint Center for Housing Studies calculates this from Census American Community Survey data. The squeeze has broadened well up the income ladder: in the Joint Center’s companion report America’s Rental Housing 2026, just over 49% of renters earning $45,000 to $74,999 were cost burdened in 2024, up 24.3 percentage points since 2001 and 9.5 points since the start of the pandemic, a group once considered largely insulated from the affordability crisis.
stats.source_label: Harvard Joint Center for Housing Studies, The State of the Nation’s Housing 2026

stats.label: Jobs lost to Chinese import competition · 1999 to 2011
stats.note: A widely cited study attributes roughly 2 million US jobs lost between 1999 and 2011 to rising imports from China, including about 985,000 in manufacturing.
stats.detail: Autor, Dorn and Hanson estimate this by comparing local labor markets more versus less exposed to import competition. Their follow-up work finds employment effects in the hardest-hit regions persisted for over a decade without full recovery, though economists debate how much of that persistence reflects trade specifically versus automation and other shocks hitting the same industries at the same time.
stats.source_label: Autor, Dorn & Hanson, NBER Working Paper 21906

stats.label: Top federal income tax rate · statutory top bracket
stats.note: The top US statutory income tax rate has fallen from 91% through the 1950s and early 1960s to 37% today.
stats.detail: This is the top marginal bracket rate, not what top earners actually paid: the 1950s bracket applied only above roughly $200,000 (about $2 million today) and came with far more deductions. The Tax Foundation puts the top 1%’s average all-in federal, state and local rate at 42.0% across the 1950s against 36.4% in 2014; Saez and Zucman, allocating corporate and estate taxes differently, find a far steeper fall for the very top. How much weight the statutory-rate story still deserves is itself contested.
stats.source_label: Tax Policy Center, historical top marginal income tax rates

stats.label: Middle-class share of national income · US households
stats.note: Middle-income households’ share of US income fell from 62% in 1970 to 42% by 2020, while their share of the population fell only from 61% to 50%.
stats.detail: Pew Research defines middle-income as two-thirds to twice the household-size-adjusted national median. The income share fell faster than the population share because income growth for middle-tier households lagged growth at the top, concentrating a shrinking pool of ‘middle’ income among a not-proportionally-smaller group of ‘middle’ households.

stats.label: CEO-to-worker pay ratio · large US firms
stats.note: CEOs at the largest US firms were paid about 281 times as much as their typical worker in 2024, up from about 21 times in 1965.
stats.detail: The Economic Policy Institute calculates this from realized CEO compensation, including exercised stock options, at the largest US public firms against average worker pay in the same industries. The ratio is volatile year to year because it tracks the stock market: it reached 372-to-1 at the 2000 peak and an all-time high of 399-to-1 in 2021, so single-year levels move more than the underlying multi-decade widening does.

questions.text: How much of four decades of widening comes from technology raising the return to skill, and how much from choices about unions, minimum wages, and top tax rates?
questions.why: The two stories imply different fixes: more skills investment, or rebuilt bargaining power. Both trends ran in parallel for decades, so crediting one crowds out the other’s claim on policy.
questions.detail:
The skills-race case treats the labor market as a race between technological change (automation, computerization, and now AI) constantly raising the payoff to scarce skills, and an education system that supplies more of them only slowly; on this view the wage gap between the credentialed and the rest is the mechanical signature of a persistent shortfall in that supply, and it predicts the gap keeps reopening with every new wave of automation regardless of what labor law does.

The institutionalist case points instead to a set of choices that moved in the same direction as the widening and could in principle be reversed: union density falling, the real value of the minimum wage eroding, and top marginal tax rates cut sharply from mid-century levels. On this view the technology story explains too little of the timing and too little of the cross-country variation, since countries with similar technology exposure diverged sharply depending on how strongly their labor-market institutions held.

questions.text: Once taxes, transfers, and income that never appears on a tax return are counted, how much has the top’s share actually risen?
questions.why: Headline top-share figures are pre-tax, pre-transfer and blind to income no return ever reports; how much of the rise survives full accounting sets how large the widening really is.
questions.detail:
The still-real side treats standard measurement adjustments as incomplete: transfers and imputed benefits close only part of the pre-tax gap, top-end income is disproportionately capital income that is easy to defer or shelter, and wealth concentration has followed a different, less-adjusted trajectory that tax-and-transfer accounting does not touch at all.

The overstated side, the core empirical claim of the Growth First Economist position, argues that once taxes paid, transfers received, and income that never appears on a filed return (fringe benefits, unrealized gains, informal income) are all counted, the rise in the top’s share and the fall in the bottom’s looks substantially smaller than the pre-tax, tax-return-only series most headline statistics use, making the trend read as more moderate and more concentrated in pockets of the distribution than a runaway divergence between the top and everyone else.

questions.text: Is a wide gap between top and bottom unjust in itself, or only when the bottom is poor, mobility is blocked, or the top’s gains were rigged?
questions.why: The answer sets the target: the width of the gap itself, or poverty, blocked mobility and rigged gains, with whatever spread survives left alone.
questions.detail:
The case that the gap itself is unjust holds that extreme concentration of income and wealth is a harm independent of anyone’s absolute standard of living, because it converts into disproportionate political power, life chances, and social standing that a democracy of equals cannot sustain; a wide gap is a problem to fix even when the bottom is comfortable.

The conditional case, closer to how the Growth First Economist and Skills Race framings read the question, holds that a wide gap earned through voluntary exchange and open competition is not itself a wrong. What is wrong is poverty, blocked mobility, or gains secured through rent-seeking, monopoly, or political capture rather than value creation, so the correct target is the floor and the fairness of the process, not the width of the spread.

questions.text: Does high inequality itself slow growth, worsen health, and distort politics, or do those harms track poverty and stalled mobility instead?
questions.why: If the harms trace to poverty and stalled mobility rather than to the gap itself, closing the gap is the wrong lever: lifting the floor would do the work.
questions.detail:
The direct-harm case argues inequality operates through channels distinct from poverty: status competition and relative deprivation affect health and social trust even among the comfortably-off, wealth concentration buys political access and regulatory capture that a merely poor-but-equal society would not produce, and extreme concentration removes purchasing power from the broad consumer base in a way that depresses aggregate demand and growth.

The poverty-root case argues the correlation between inequality and these harms is confounded: what actually damages health, growth, and political trust is being poor, insecure, or stuck, not the mere existence of a large gap to people far above you, so a society that closed mobility gaps and lifted the floor could carry a wide top-to-bottom spread with none of the harms usually blamed on inequality itself.

questions.text: Should policy aim at the top’s share, the bottom’s floor, or the middle’s shrinking claim on national income?
questions.why: The three targets are not one project: each reaches for different instruments, and some of those instruments work against each other.
questions.detail:
Aiming at the top treats concentration itself, especially unearned or rigged gains, as the target, and reaches for capital taxation, inheritance taxes, and antitrust, the last of these the Market Power Trustbuster’s lever, aimed at rents taken in product and labor markets before a paycheck is ever written. Aiming at the floor treats destitution and insecurity as the target regardless of how tall the top is, and reaches for minimum wages, wage subsidies, and safety-net generosity, a framing closer to the Growth First Economist’s absolute-standard-of-living view.

Aiming at the middle treats the shrinking claim of median earners on national income, rather than either tail, as the real story, and points toward rebuilding the wage and job structure that used to sit between the bottom and the top, closer to the Worker Power Institutionalist and Trade Shock Reindustrialist framings. Because these three targets can require different, sometimes competing, instruments, choosing among them is a live political choice, not a technical detail.

questions.text: Is the binding constraint on living standards how income is distributed, or the price of housing, care, and energy?
questions.why: If the squeeze is the price of housing, care and energy rather than the shape of the distribution, redistribution without more supply leaves households bidding up the same scarce goods.
questions.detail:
The living-costs case, the Abundance Builder position, argues stagnant purchasing power is driven less by how income is divided and more by supply constraints in a handful of large, hard-to-substitute categories: housing near jobs, childcare and eldercare, and energy, so expanding supply there would raise real living standards even for households whose income share hasn’t moved, while redistribution alone leaves them bidding up the same constrained supply.

The distribution case holds that even generous supply-side fixes cannot substitute for how much income households have to begin with, that the same supply constraints bind hardest on low earners because they have the least room to absorb price increases, and that treating the cost side as the whole story risks leaving the underlying income and wealth concentration untouched while crediting supply reforms with gains a fairer distribution would have delivered directly.

questions.text: Do wage-setting institutions and stronger competition for workers compress the distribution more durably than taxes and transfers after the fact?
questions.why: Shaping wages before the paycheck and redistributing after it are not equally durable levers; which one holds a compressed distribution without constant political renewal is contested.
questions.detail:
The pre-market case, aligned with the Worker Power Institutionalist position, holds that wage floors, union bargaining coverage, and tight labor markets that force employers to compete for workers change the distribution at its source, so the compression persists without an annual political fight over tax rates, and survives changes of government better than a redistribution regime the next administration’s tax bill can unwind.

The redistribute-after case holds that pre-market interventions distort hiring and wage-setting and are limited by how much bargaining power can realistically be rebuilt in a globalized, automated economy, whereas taxes and transfers can be dialed to hit a chosen distributional target directly and adjusted precisely, making them the more reliable and measurable lever even if they require sustained political will to maintain.

questions.text: How much of the hollowed middle is import competition and offshoring, and can tariffs or industrial policy rebuild those rungs?
questions.why: Trade and automation compete as the explanation for the hollowed middle of the wage ladder, and they point to different remedies: retraining, or tariffs and rebuilt domestic production.
questions.detail:
The trade-driven case, the Trade Shock Reindustrialist position, holds that the sudden opening of low-wage manufacturing competition and the offshoring it enabled destroyed specifically the middle-skill, middle-wage production jobs anchoring the wage ladder, concentrated by region and industry in a way a smooth technology trend would not produce, and argues that rebuilding domestic production capacity through tariffs or industrial policy is the direct way to restore those rungs.

The skeptical case argues trade is at most a partial, regionally concentrated contributor next to automation’s broader, more diffuse effect on middle-skill work, that tariffs and industrial policy have a mixed record of reviving the jobs they target rather than just raising prices, and that even successful reindustrialization would face the same automation pressure that hollowed out manufacturing employment even in countries that never lost production to trade.

questions.text: Can a wealth or billionaire minimum tax be collected at scale, or do valuation, avoidance, and mobility erode the base?
questions.why: The argument is not whether such a tax is desirable but whether it can be assessed and collected before valuation fights, avoidance and mobility hollow out the base.
questions.detail:
The collectible case, the Capital Tax Egalitarian position’s implementation claim, points to existing models such as property-tax assessment, mark-to-market treatment of publicly traded securities, and information-reporting regimes as evidence that illiquid and hard-to-value assets can be assessed with acceptable error, and that international coordination can close the exit routes that undermined earlier wealth-tax experiments.

The erosion case points to the historical record of wealth taxes being repealed or narrowed across the countries that tried them, largely over valuation disputes for privately held businesses and art, and the ease with which very mobile, very wealthy individuals and their capital relocate to lower-tax jurisdictions, arguing that a tax raising little relative to its administrative cost and political durability is not a real solution regardless of its rate on paper.

positions.name: Worker Power Institutionalist
positions.steelman: Inequality is a policy choice: rebuild bargaining power, and the gap narrows.
positions.description: Pay is set at a bargaining table, and for four decades American workers have negotiated from an emptier hand. Union coverage fell from 27.0% of US workers in 1979 to 11.6% by 2019, the federal minimum wage lost about 40% of its real value since its 1968 peak, and the top tax rate fell from 91% to 37%. None of that was inevitable. It was legislated, and it can be legislated back.
positions.detail:
Between 1945 and 1980, the United States combined its highest union density with its most broadly shared growth in modern history: the postwar “Great Compression” that Claudia Goldin and Robert Margo first named and quantified. This camp treats that period not as a lucky accident but as proof of concept, and Farber, Herbst, Kuziemko and Naidu’s 2021 Quarterly Journal of Economics study extends the argument in both directions. Tracing a century of Gallup micro-data on union membership, they find a household union premium holding steady between ten and twenty log points across enormous changes in who joined, and consistent evidence that unions reduce inequality, explaining a significant share of the fall in inequality between the mid-1930s and the late 1940s, which this camp reads as bargaining power, not the supply of schooling, doing the work.

The disagreement inside this camp is less about whether institutions matter than about which lever to pull first. Economic Policy Institute economists such as Lawrence Mishel, Josh Bivens and Elise Gould push hardest on rebuilding sectoral or multi-employer bargaining so gains reach nonunion workers too, since only 5.9% of private-sector workers now carry a union card. Others, in the tradition of David Card and Alan Krueger’s minimum-wage research, treat the wage floor as the more portable, faster-enacted tool: their 1994 finding that a New Jersey minimum-wage increase cost no fast-food jobs relative to neighboring Pennsylvania broke a settled consensus and reoriented the field. A newer strand, building on Piketty, Saez and Stantcheva’s bargaining-elasticity model, extends the same logic upward: cutting the top tax rate does not just fail to raise effort, it raises the payoff to bargaining harder for a fixed pool of profit, which makes restoring higher top rates a wage-floor policy aimed at the other end of the distribution.

Proponents keep returning to the same cross-country fact: rich democracies faced broadly similar technology and trade exposure over the same decades, yet inequality rose far less where bargaining coverage held, much of continental Europe, than where it collapsed, the U.S. and U.K. Sociologist Jake Rosenfeld makes the culture-and-power version of the case in What Unions No Longer Do: unions did not just raise wages, they set norms of fairness that bounded how much a workplace could tolerate at the top, and once that boundary went, so did the restraint.
positions.proponents: Economic Policy Institute (Lawrence Mishel, Josh Bivens, Elise Gould), Henry Farber, Ilyana Kuziemko, Suresh Naidu, Jake Rosenfeld, David Card, Thomas Piketty, Emmanuel Saez
positions.representative_note: Its union-decline decompositions (a 7.7-point widening of the 90/50 wage gap traced to deunionization) are this position’s most-cited empirical anchor.
positions.prevalence_basis: Anchors a large empirical literature on unions, minimum wages and the pay-productivity gap, much of it produced by labor-aligned research institutes such as the Economic Policy Institute; minimum-wage and collective-bargaining law recurs as a legislative item across rich democracies.

positions.name: Skills Race Theorist
positions.steelman: The demand for skill keeps outrunning the supply schools and training produce.
positions.description: Invest in people rather than fight over slices of a fixed pie: supply the skills technology rewards and the gap narrows. The college pay gap widened faster after 1979 than in the decades before. Autor, Goldin and Katz put 62% of that speed-up on a slowdown in the supply of graduates, and 38% on technology raising demand for skill. So widen college and vocational pipelines, and treat AI as the next lap of the same race.
positions.detail:
The Autor, Goldin and Katz accounting is the number this camp keeps returning to: 62% of the post-1979 acceleration in the college wage premium’s growth rate, relative to 1939 to 1979, traces to the slowdown in the relative supply of college graduates, with the other 38% owed to faster skill-biased demand. Goldin and Katz put the same point in growth rates: the relative supply of college workers grew 3.89% a year from 1960 to 1980 but only 2.27% a year from 1980 to 2005, a deceleration that on their accounting “more than fully explains” the post-1980 rise in the college wage premium. That is why the prescription runs toward supply, widening access and completion, rather than toward taxing and redistributing after wages are already set.

Tinbergen described the race first, in a 1974 Kyklos paper on the substitution of graduate by other labor. Katz and Murphy formalized it in 1992 by modeling the relative supply and demand for skilled labor, and Goldin and Katz extended it into a full economic history in their 2008 book, tracing US wage structure back to the pace of high school and college expansion over the twentieth century. Autor, Levy, and Murnane then sharpened the mechanism in 2003, showing computers substitute for routine, codifiable tasks specifically rather than rewarding skill in general, which is why the middle of the wage ladder hollowed out even as both the top and the low-skill service sector grew.

Where the camp disagrees is about what happens now. The college wage premium’s growth flattened after roughly 2000, and a 2025 San Francisco Fed working paper attributes the stall to a slowdown in skill-biased demand itself and rising substitutability between college and non-college workers, pushing some toward vocational pipelines, apprenticeships, and the social skills economist David Deming finds employers now price up alongside technical ones. A newer, more unsettled fight concerns AI: in 2024 Autor argued it could help rebuild the middle class by putting expert tasks, medical triage, legal drafting, routine coding, within reach of less credentialed workers it augments, which would compress rather than widen the premium; this camp treats that as the next lap of the race, not grounds to abandon the framework.
positions.proponents: Claudia Goldin, Lawrence Katz, David Autor, Jan Tinbergen, Frank Levy, Richard Murnane
positions.representative_note: MIT labor economist behind the task-based framework explaining automation’s uneven effect on routine versus skilled work, now studying how AI itself could reshape, and possibly compress, the skill premium.
positions.prevalence_basis: The supply-and-demand framework Tinbergen, Katz, Goldin and Autor built into a standard reference point in labor economics, matched by an education-and-training footprint in national policy and now extended to evidence on AI exposure by occupation.

positions.name: Capital Tax Egalitarian
positions.steelman: Wealth compounds faster than the economy grows, and it is taxed lighter than a paycheck.
positions.description: Fortunes that sit and compound should not be taxed more lightly than wages. Whenever the return on capital outruns growth, wealth concentrates on its own, and a tax built on wages misses unrealized gains and inheritance. ProPublica’s leaked IRS files put the 25 richest Americans’ true tax rate at 3.4% on $401 billion of gains from 2014 to 2018. So tax the fortune, not only the income it realizes.
positions.detail:
Thomas Piketty’s contribution was to make the mechanism visible: across two centuries of data, the after-tax return on capital has run persistently above the economy’s growth rate, so wealth accumulated in the past grows faster than wealth earned in the present can catch up. That is why this camp treats the top’s share as a stock problem, not a flow problem — cutting income tax rates on wages does nothing to it, because the wages were never where the concentration was happening.

Emmanuel Saez and Gabriel Zucman turned the theory into an accounting exercise in The Triumph of Injustice, tallying every tax paid at every level of government and finding the 400 richest US households paying a lower effective rate than teachers, steelworkers, and retirees for the first time in a century — a finding ProPublica’s leaked-return investigation then made concrete at the individual level, down to Bezos’s 1.1% true tax rate on $127 billion of wealth growth. Internally the camp argues hardest over collection, not diagnosis: France repealed its wealth tax in 2017 after years of argument over capital flight, and although the government’s own France Stratégie evaluation committee found departures falling sharply after the 2018 reform, averaging 260 departures a year against 380 returns among wealth-tax payers from 2018 to 2021, against 950 departures a year against 370 returns in the ISF years from 2011 to 2016, critics inside the tradition, not just outside it, treat the repeal as a real design failure to answer rather than dismiss. The response has been to move from a blunt annual levy toward mechanisms designed to survive mobility and valuation problems — exit taxes, third-party asset reporting, and coordinated minimums so no single jurisdiction bears the flight risk alone. Zucman’s 2024 G20 blueprint, commissioned by Brazil’s presidency, is the current test case: it starts from billionaires’ measured 0.3% effective rate on wealth and proposes a coordinated 2% minimum, projected to raise $200–250 billion a year from the roughly 3,000 people it would touch. Elizabeth Warren and Bernie Sanders built US presidential-campaign wealth-tax plans directly on Saez and Zucman’s modeling, and Oxfam has run with the same arithmetic to argue for taxing inherited fortunes at the point of transfer, not just income at the point of receipt.
positions.proponents: Thomas Piketty, Emmanuel Saez, Gabriel Zucman, Elizabeth Warren, Bernie Sanders, Oxfam
positions.representative_note: UC Berkeley / Paris School of Economics economist behind the 2024 G20 blueprint for a coordinated 2% global minimum tax on billionaire wealth
positions.prevalence_basis: Built on Piketty’s Capital in the Twenty-First Century, one of the most widely discussed economics books of the past decade, and carried by an active G20 track on a minimum effective tax for billionaires, commissioned by Brazil’s 2024 presidency and publicly backed by governments including Brazil, France, Spain and South Africa.

positions.name: Growth First Economist
positions.steelman: Count taxes and transfers and the top’s after-tax income share has barely moved since 1960.
positions.description: What counts is whether living standards are rising and whether a poor kid can still climb, not the top’s slice this year. Census surveys leave out taxes, most transfers and employer benefits, so the headline gap measures the wrong thing. From IRS records, Auten and Splinter put the top 1%’s after-tax share at 8.8% in 2019, 0.2 points above its 8.6% in 1962. Growth, not the gap, is the yardstick.
positions.detail:
This camp took shape as a direct rebuttal to the top-income-share estimates that Thomas Piketty, Emmanuel Saez and Gabriel Zucman built into the World Inequality Database in the 2000s and 2010s, numbers that entered political speech as settled fact: the top 1% supposedly capturing the lion’s share of growth since the 1970s. The rebuttal’s core move is accounting, not ideology: those estimates used pre-tax, pre-transfer, tax-unit income, so they missed Social Security, Medicaid and Medicare, food assistance, the EITC, and employer-sponsored health coverage, all of which have grown enormously and disproportionately reach lower incomes. The Congressional Budget Office’s own distributional tables, tracking income after federal taxes and transfers, show the bottom and middle quintiles gaining substantially since 1979, not stagnating.

The camp is not monolithic in how far it pushes the claim. Gerald Auten and David Splinter, publishing in the Journal of Political Economy and government economists by trade (Treasury and the Joint Committee on Taxation), keep close to the peer-reviewed center: their after-tax top 1% share is essentially flat since the 1960s once underreported income, corporate and estate taxes, and transfers are properly allocated. Phil Gramm, Robert Ekelund and John Early, in the Hayek Prize-winning The Myth of American Inequality, argue further that bottom-quintile real income grew by hundreds of percent from 1967 to 2017 once the Census’s own excluded transfers are added back, a figure that has drawn sharper methodological pushback (imputing Medicaid and Medicare dollar-for-dollar as cash-equivalent income, treatment of household size) than the Auten-Splinter work has. Scott Winship, who directs the American Enterprise Institute’s Center on Opportunity and Social Mobility, occupies the middle ground, pairing the tax-data corrections with consumption and mobility measures to argue growth and opportunity, not the shape of the distribution, are what a poor household actually experiences.

Critics, including the original WID.world team, reply that even the corrected numbers still show pre-tax market inequality rising sharply, and that a stable after-tax share only proves the tax-and-transfer system is offsetting a growing market-driven gap, not that the gap doesn’t exist. This camp’s answer is that offsetting the gap is exactly what a well-functioning system is supposed to do, so the redistribution critics want is, to a significant degree, already happening: the debate should move from how unequal pre-tax America looks to whether growth and mobility for people actually living there are improving, which by this camp’s reading they are.
positions.proponents: Gerald Auten, David Splinter, Phil Gramm, Robert Ekelund, John Early, Scott Winship (American Enterprise Institute)
positions.representative_note: Treasury and Joint Committee on Taxation economists whose IRS-tax-data reconstruction of income shares, accounting for taxes and transfers, anchors this camp’s rebuttal to the standard rising-inequality narrative.
positions.prevalence_basis: Institutional backing from market-liberal think tanks, and a contested top-share series produced by Treasury and Joint Committee on Taxation economists that has been argued over in the top journals since 2024.

positions.name: Trade Shock Reindustrialist
positions.steelman: Trade policy hollowed the wage ladder one factory town at a time, and it never grew back.
positions.description: A country that stops making things stops offering workers without a degree a ladder up: factory jobs paid wages and benefits the service economy never replaced. The China shock was a policy choice, above all China’s 2001 WTO entry. Autor, Dorn and Hanson find the hardest-hit zones still short on manufacturing jobs in 2019. The fix runs through production: tariffs and industrial policy.
positions.detail:
For decades, mainstream trade economics treated import competition as a wash: some workers lose, others gain in export sectors or cheaper goods, and the net is close to costless once markets reallocate labor. Autor, Dorn and Hanson’s “China Syndrome” research broke that consensus. Tracking commuting zones by their exposure to Chinese import growth after China’s 2001 WTO entry, they found manufacturing job losses that did not get soaked up by other local employment or out-migration, wage declines concentrated in the bottom four deciles, and effects that spilled outside manufacturing entirely. Economic Policy Institute estimates built on the same trade data put the cumulative toll at millions of jobs eliminated or displaced, rising with every update as the deficit widened.

The camp is not one bloc. Its labor-left wing (Robert Scott and EPI, the United Steelworkers) wants managed trade, tariffs on dumped goods and rebuilt union power. Its national-conservative wing (Oren Cass and American Compass, the Coalition for a Prosperous America) wants tariffs paired with industrial policy and reshoring incentives, explicitly breaking with the free-trade orthodoxy of their own party. Both draw on the same underlying finding: that trade’s losers were concentrated, working-class and left with nowhere else to go. That convergence, an economics usually coded left and a nationalism usually coded right agreeing that Washington chose this outcome and can choose differently, is what gives the position its current political weight.

The strongest evidence is the persistence finding: the 2021 follow-up work showed trade-exposed regions still carrying depressed manufacturing employment, lower employment-to-population ratios and lower income per capita in 2019, with no sign of the self-correction basic trade theory predicted. Researchers in this vein also linked the same exposure map to rising opioid mortality, falling fertility, falling marriage rates among young men and the 2016 swing toward Trump in the hardest-hit counties, a much wider social bill than a jobs number alone. Even economists who doubt manufacturing can be rebuilt at the old scale, given automation and a labor force now more service-heavy, concede the shock itself was real and geographically brutal, which is why the argument inside the camp is over the size and shape of the rebuild, not whether one is owed.
positions.proponents: Robert Scott (Economic Policy Institute), Oren Cass (American Compass), Michael Stumo (Coalition for a Prosperous America), United Steelworkers
positions.representative_note: American Compass founder; the leading voice reframing reindustrialization as the remedy for a hollowed wage ladder
positions.prevalence_basis: The “China shock” papers are among the most-cited empirical work in the field, and tariffs plus industrial policy have been live US policy rather than proposal since 2025.

positions.name: Market Power Trustbuster
positions.steelman: A few dominant firms take their cut in higher prices and lower wages first.
positions.description: The gap is not only what the market produced, it is what dominant firms took in higher prices and lower wages on the way through. De Loecker, Eeckhout and Unger find average US markups rose from 21% above cost in 1980 to 61% by 2016, and Philippon estimates weak competition leaves the median household’s purchasing power more than $5,000 a year short of what it would be if markets had stayed competitive. The lever is competition policy, not a transfer after the fact: block mergers, void non-competes, enforce the laws on the books.
positions.detail:
The diagnosis is old antitrust doctrine returned. Louis Brandeis argued that concentrated private power is a political problem and not only an economic one, a view narrowed almost out of existence once antitrust was reduced to a consumer-price test in the 1980s. Joseph Stiglitz made rents the organizing idea of The Price of Inequality, arguing that much of what accrues at the top is wealth transferred from everyone else rather than wealth created, and Thomas Philippon’s The Great Reversal supplied the cross-Atlantic comparison, finding US markets have grown less competitive than Europe’s since the 1990s. David Autor, David Dorn, Lawrence Katz, Christina Patterson and John Van Reenen supplied the macro link in their superstar-firms work: industries where concentration rose most saw the largest declines in labor’s share of value added, driven by reallocation toward large, low-labor-share firms rather than by pay falling inside firms.

The camp divides over how much of that concentration is power and how much is efficiency. The Brandeisian wing, the Open Markets Institute, Lina Khan and Marshall Steinbaum, treats scale itself as a standing danger to workers and to democracy and wants structural remedies: breakups, merger blocks, and bans on non-compete and no-poach agreements. A more conventionally economic wing accepts that superstar firms may genuinely be more productive and would target enforcement at demonstrable rents, especially in labor markets, where the monopsony evidence is now strong. Critics press hardest on the markup estimates themselves: markups inferred from accounting data depend on which costs count as variable, and James Traina finds a far smaller increase once selling and administrative expenses are treated as costs of production.

What holds the camp together is where it locates the fix. Rents are taken upstream, in the prices households pay and the wages employers offer, so neither a rebuilt bargaining table nor a tax on accumulated fortunes reaches them at the source. When Open Markets convened policymakers, researchers and strategists in Washington in June 2026 around concentrated private power as the central axis of political economy, it was a measure of how far the argument has traveled from the antitrust bar into ordinary politics.
positions.proponents: Joseph Stiglitz, Thomas Philippon, Marshall Steinbaum, Lina Khan, Open Markets Institute, Roosevelt Institute
positions.representative_note: Washington research and advocacy institute arguing that concentrated corporate power, in product and labor markets alike, moves income upward before wages are ever set.
positions.prevalence_basis: A revived antitrust tradition with a measured empirical base in rising markups, labor-market concentration and monopsony, and a live policy footprint in merger-guideline revision and the fight over non-compete bans; a smaller share of the inequality literature than the union or skills accounts.

positions.name: Abundance Builder
positions.steelman: Fix the price of housing, care and energy, and the squeeze eases — gap or no gap.
positions.description: What decides whether a family gets ahead is whether the paycheck clears rent, day care and the power bill. Zoning, permitting delays and licensing throttle the supply of what poorer households spend most on: the poorest tenth of households spends 26.2% of its budget on housing, the richest tenth 18.5%. Redistribution alone bids up a fixed supply; Houston and Tokyo kept building, and kept costs down.
positions.detail:
The label is new; the diagnosis is not. Economists studying why housing costs diverged between similarly booming cities laid the groundwork years before ‘abundance’ became a buzzword: Edward Glaeser and Joseph Gyourko’s research tied the gap directly to how tightly local land-use rules constrained new construction. The YIMBY housing movement translated that research into local politics through the 2010s; writers then generalized it, first as ‘supply-side progressivism’ (Matthew Yglesias, Jerusalem Demsas and the Niskanen Center, from around 2021), then as the broader ‘abundance agenda’ once Ezra Klein and Derek Thompson’s Abundance became a bestseller in 2025. Yoni Appelbaum’s Stuck extended the argument to geographic mobility itself, arguing that frozen housing supply is what stopped Americans from moving toward opportunity the way earlier generations did.

The camp is not united on method. Klein, Thompson and the Niskanen Center push a deregulatory reading: strip away permitting delays, environmental review used as a veto and occupational licensing, and private builders will supply what’s needed. Marc Dunkelman’s Why Nothing Works takes a more institutional view, arguing that decades of reforms meant to check unaccountable power, like Robert Moses’s, left behind a process so procedurally hedged that even well-funded, well-intentioned public projects can’t get built, so the fix has to restore capacity to execute, not just remove rules. On care specifically, the debate sharpens further: child care and eldercare are labor-intensive, so building ‘supply’ also means raising pay for a workforce chronically underpaid relative to its credentials, a point advocates from the care side of the coalition press harder than the housing side does.

The clearest natural experiment is jurisdictional. Houston, with no citywide zoning code, and Tokyo, under national by-right zoning rules that limit local veto power, have both kept homebuilding roughly in step with population and job growth for decades, while in tightly zoned San Francisco prices have pulled hundreds of thousands of dollars clear of what building actually costs. That San Francisco wedge is the ‘zoning tax’ Glaeser and Gyourko measure across US metros as the gap between a home’s price and the cost of producing it, and this camp reads the pattern as evidence that the housing shortage, not income inequality per se, is the proximate cause of the affordability squeeze on the bottom half of the distribution.
positions.proponents: Ezra Klein, Derek Thompson, Jerusalem Demsas, Yoni Appelbaum, Matthew Yglesias, Edward Glaeser, Niskanen Center (Steven Teles, Samuel Hammond, Daniel Takash)
positions.representative_note: The book that turned a decade of YIMBY and supply-side-progressive arguments into a mainstream political label, arguing scarcity of housing, energy and infrastructure, not income inequality per se, is liberalism’s central self-inflicted wound.
positions.prevalence_basis: Thin in the older inequality literature but rising fast: a 2025 bestseller whose framing has since been taken up across mainstream affordability politics.

positions.name: Family Structure Analyst
positions.steelman: Family stability predicts a child’s income better than the tax code does.
positions.description: A child’s shot at climbing starts at home, not in the tax code. Chetty and coauthors find the share of single-parent households in a community predicts a poor child’s odds of reaching the top better than school quality, segregation or local inequality. Marriage pools two incomes, two sets of time and two buffers against a job loss, and its retreat is steepest among Americans without a degree.
positions.detail:
This case traces to Daniel Patrick Moynihan’s 1965 report and William Julius Wilson’s work on the vanishing two-parent Black family, but it moved from sociology into mainstream economics with Chetty, Hendren, Kline and Saez’s 2014 ‘Where Is the Land of Opportunity?’, which found the share of single parents in a commuting zone predicted a poor child’s upward mobility more powerfully than school quality, racial segregation, or the area’s own income inequality. Melissa Kearney’s 2023 book The Two-Parent Privilege pressed the same finding into a full economic argument: the fifty-year retreat from marriage, concentrated almost entirely among Americans without a four-year degree, has widened the gap in household resources, parental time, and children’s eventual earnings even as marriage rates among college graduates barely moved.

The camp splits on the fix. W. Bradford Wilcox and Robert Lerman at the Institute for Family Studies and AEI push the ‘success sequence’: finish school, get a job, marry, then have children, in that order. Wendy Wang and Wilcox report that 97% of millennials who followed all three steps are not poor by their mid-30s, and Lerman and Wilcox’s For Richer, For Poorer puts the annual intact-family income premium at $6,500 for young men and $4,700 for young women. Kearney and Isabel Sawhill at Brookings are warier of moralizing about marriage directly and argue instead for the economic footing, stable jobs, wage growth, occupational licensing reform, that makes viable households possible again, holding that family formation responds to opportunity as much as opportunity responds to family formation.

Critics inside and outside the camp press the endogeneity problem hard: does family breakdown cause low income, or does low income, via job loss, mass incarceration, or the retreat of blue-collar wages since the 1970s, cause family breakdown? Kearney answers with the fracking boom, where a local surge in the earnings of men without a degree raised births but left marriage rates and single motherhood largely unmoved, which she reads as evidence that the retreat from marriage is not simply downstream of men’s wages, but the camp concedes the causal arrows likely run both ways, and treats family stability as a lever worth pulling regardless of how much of the inequality trend it explains on its own.
positions.proponents: W. Bradford Wilcox, Melissa S. Kearney, Robert I. Lerman, Isabel Sawhill, Ron Haskins (Brookings)
positions.representative_note: University of Maryland economist whose book turned Chetty’s mobility findings into the fullest economic case that family structure, not just income, has split the classes.
positions.prevalence_basis: A smaller footprint in economics than in sociology and family policy, sustained by Melissa Kearney’s prominent 2023 book on two-parent households and durable conservative policy backing.

crux.lead: The split runs twice: what pulled the ends apart, then whether the distance is the harm.
crux.lead_highlight: whether the distance is the harm
crux.subtitle: Six camps name the force that pulled the ends apart: bargaining rules, the skill race, compounding capital, market power, trade, the household. Two say the measured distance was never the injury.
crux.empirical: Decomposition: how much of four decades each force explains, and whether the top’s rise survives counting taxes, transfers and income that never reaches a tax return. Then whether the distance harms of its own accord once poverty and blocked mobility are held constant, and whether wage floors compress more durably than transfers.
crux.values: Whether a wide distance is unjust in itself, or only when the bottom is poor, mobility is blocked, or the top’s gains were rigged. Beneath that sits what policy owes whom: the top’s share, the bottom’s floor, or the middle’s claim — and whether a household’s own arrangements are a private matter or a public one.

actions.title: Economic Policy Institute
actions.description: Research institute making the case that eroded unions, a stagnant minimum wage, and lower top tax rates, not just technology, drove the wage gap, and pushing to rebuild labor standards.

actions.title: National Skills Coalition
actions.description: Workforce coalition documenting how digital and technical skill gaps widen pay differences, and pushing states to target public funds at closing them.

actions.title: Patriotic Millionaires
actions.description: Network of wealthy Americans lobbying for higher taxes on capital income and inheritance and for a coordinated global minimum tax on billionaires.

actions.title: The Myth of American Inequality
actions.description: Book and AEI discussion arguing that once taxes and transfer payments are counted, measured income inequality is far smaller than headline Census figures suggest.

actions.title: Coalition for a Prosperous America
actions.description: Manufacturer and labor coalition pushing tariff reform to rebuild domestic industrial capacity and the wage ladder it once supported.

actions.title: Open Markets Institute
actions.description: Anti-monopoly research and advocacy group documenting how concentration in product and labor markets raises prices and holds down wages, and pressing for structural antitrust enforcement.

actions.title: YIMBY Action
actions.description: National network of local pro-housing chapters organizing to build enough homes to bring down housing costs directly, rather than through redistribution.

actions.title: Institute for Family Studies
actions.description: Family-policy research site publishing evidence that children who experience more family instability see lower earnings and mobility as adults.
